newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt charges militants with planning Cairo attacks.
newsitem.headline: Egypt charges militants with planning Cairo attacks.

text.p: Egyptian State Security prosecutors on Thursday charged 21 suspected Moslem militants with planning to attack coffee shops and video clubs in Cairo on the order of an imprisoned comrade, security sources said.

They said the men, allegedly members of al-Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group), had been ordered to carry out the attacks by Gama'a leader Sameh Sallam in order to resume the group's activity in the capital.
The Gama'a last staged an attack in Cairo in April 1996 when it claimed responsibility for the massacre of 18 Greek tourists outside a hotel.
Bloody police crackdowns have largely confined Gama'a activity over the past couple of years to the south of Egypt.
Prosecutors said Sallam had issued the orders for the attacks through people who came to visit him in jail.

Police arrested the 21 suspected militants two weeks ago and seized weapons and ammunition that prosecutors said would have been used in the attacks in crowded areas in north Cairo, the sources said. The militants have also been charged with joining an illegal organisation.
Prosecutors did not say when Sallam issued the alleged orders.
Six imprisoned Gama'a leaders issued a statement last month calling on followers to stop unilaterally all violent acts.

The appeal, read out by an alleged militant at a trial last month, was rejected by exiled Gama'a leaders who said they would continue their armed struggle to transform Egypt into a strict Moslem state.
More than 1,000 people have been killed since the group took up arms in 1992 to overthrow the government and transform Egypt into a strict Islamic state.

Police say they have broken the back of the military wing of the Gama'a through crackdowns and the number of attacks has declined sharply since the mid-1990s, when the militants were killing about one policeman a day.
